quiz_questions: The strategy rejects wrapping the operating system's existing word-count utility, even though that utility already counts words. Explain what would go wrong with that approach, and which of the strategy's goals or success criteria it would undermine.
Why does the strategy build the command without a third-party command-line framework?

The Quality Gate commands are listed as a dependency whose status is 'not yet defined'. If they stayed undefined, which of the strategy's success criteria could no longer be verified in the way the strategy describes, and why? Consider how the criteria are measured and how often they are checked.
quiz_answers: Wrapping the OS utility makes behavior depend on the platform: the utility is missing on some systems and counts differently on others, so the same file could give different counts on different machines, and the counting couldn't be tested in isolation. That undermines Goal 1 and the "Word-count correctness" criterion (100% of agreed fixtures match, checked by automated tests every change), Goal 2 (a missing utility is a failure the tool doesn't control, not a clear one-line error), Goal 4 (a new user's machine may lack the utility, so the README alone wouldn't be enough), and the core strategy of building only on what the language runtime provides.

AGENTS.md requires a documented rationale for every external dependency, and a single-argument command gains too little from a framework to justify the added install weight, lockfile churn and supply-chain surface.

Three criteria lose their verification. "Word-count correctness" is measured by automated tests "every change, via the Quality Gate", and "Graceful error handling" by automated tests every change; with no defined test command, nothing runs those tests on each change, so neither can be verified as described. "Quality Gate defined and green" fails outright, since its target is 4 defined, passing commands and it would stay at the baseline of 0 (Goal 3 too). The other two aren't affected: "Runtime dependency footprint" is checked at each review in pyproject.toml, and "Documented onboarding" is a manual run before each release, so neither depends on the Quality Gate.
quiz_justification: Both answers show real understanding of the strategy's reasoning. On the rejected OS-utility alternative, the reviewer explained why platform dependence matters and traced it to the correctness, error-handling and onboarding commitments. On the undefined Quality Gate dependency, the reviewer reasoned from each criterion's measurement method and cadence. They identified which criteria lose their verification path and correctly excluded the two that do not depend on the gate. No significant reasoning gaps were found. The only nuance is that the error-handling criterion's cadence says 'every change' without naming the gate explicitly, but inferring that the gate runs those tests is a sound reading of the strategy.
quiz_notes: The answer explains the mechanism: the utility is missing or behaves differently across platforms, so the same file could produce different counts and counting could not be tested in isolation. It ties this to specific commitments: 100% fixture correctness under automated tests, the clear-error goal (a missing utility is a failure the tool cannot control), README-only onboarding, and the runtime-only core strategy. This shows the non-adjacent consequences of the rejection rather than only restating the tradeoff sentence.

The answer correctly identifies the three affected criteria: Word-count correctness, Graceful error handling and Quality Gate defined and green. It reasons from their measurement and cadence: without a defined test command, nothing runs the automated tests on every change, and the gate criterion stays at its baseline of 0. It also correctly excludes the dependency-footprint and onboarding criteria, because they are checked at review and manually before release, independently of the gate. The exclusion shows real reasoning about how verification works, not just a list.

quiz_questions: The spec reads input with strict UTF-8 decoding and treats invalid bytes as an error with exit 1. What would go wrong if the command instead decoded with errors="replace" and carried on?

The spec keeps the word rule in hello.counter.count_words(text) with no file, process or console I/O, and puts reading, decoding, printing and exit codes in hello.cli. Suppose a later change makes count_words accept a path and open the file itself. Explain what this would break or make harder, both for testing the word rule and for the reuse the spec anticipates, and why the architecture test bans those imports rather than relying on convention.

Under the CLI error contract, a missing file, an unreadable path and invalid UTF-8 all exit with status 1, while a wrong argument count exits with status 2 via argparse. What does this split let a calling script do, and what did the spec knowingly give up?
quiz_answers: Invalid bytes would become U+FFFD replacement characters, which are non-whitespace, so a garbled or wrongly encoded file would silently print a plausible-looking count with exit 0 instead of reporting that it is not valid UTF-8 text.

Testing: the word rule would be testable only through real files. Today count_words("one two three") and the empty/whitespace cases run in memory; with a path, every rule test needs temporary files and drags in encoding and file errors, so a failure no longer tells you whether the rule or the I/O is wrong. It also blurs ownership: word-counter explicitly does not own file access, encoding or errors, while word-count-command owns turning missing, unreadable and undecodable files into one-line messages. Opening files in count_words would leak FileNotFoundError or UnicodeDecodeError from the wrong layer, or duplicate that handling. Reuse: ADR-0002 expects future utilities to reuse the counter, and they may have text from somewhere other than a file; a path-only function forces them to write a file first. Why a test instead of convention: a convention erodes silently, one convenient import at a time. The architecture test (ADR-0002, DETERMINISTIC, tests/arch/test_layering.py bans os, sys, pathlib, io, open and subprocess) runs in the Quality Gate on every change and fails the moment the boundary is crossed. It is also listed as a regression guardrail.

A script can tell 'the command was invoked wrongly' (2) apart from 'the command ran but the file could not be used' (1), but it cannot tell which file problem occurred without reading the stderr message.
quiz_justification: The reviewer understood why the word counter is pure. It lets the word rule be tested in memory, without files. It keeps error ownership in the command layer, which protects the one-line error contract. It allows reuse with text that does not come from a file. The reviewer also understood why the boundary is enforced by a deterministic architecture test instead of a convention: conventions erode one convenient import at a time, and the test catches a violation on every gate run. Nothing significant was missed. The answer goes beyond restating the spec by explaining how a path-taking counter would undermine the error contract owned by hello.cli.
quiz_notes: The answer covers all three parts of the question. Testing: rule tests would need temporary files, and encoding and file errors would mix into them, so a failure would no longer show whether the rule or the I/O is at fault. Reuse: future utilities may get text from somewhere other than a file, and a path-only function would force them to write one first. Enforcement: a convention erodes silently, while the deterministic layering test fails in the Quality Gate the moment the boundary is crossed. The answer also notes a consequence that is not next to the decision: FileNotFoundError or UnicodeDecodeError would surface from the wrong layer, or the one-line error handling owned by word-count-command would have to be duplicated.
